rationale: Evidence: both races ended off track in all 60 development trials. Iteration 1 widened the array and softened the controller, and progress improved only slightly (s-bend 0.04 to 0.14, oval 0.15 to 0.14, slalom 0.04 to 0.10). Line loss is still about 0.85-1 event per run on s-bend and slalom. The off-track limit (max_error about 0.06-0.068) is reached while rms_error is only about 0.024-0.03. Steering oscillation is low (0.06-0.14), so the robot is not jittering; it drifts steadily away from the line. The most likely cause is a steady bias: the fixed left/right motor mismatch pushes the robot one way, and with ki = 0 a proportional controller holds a residual offset of roughly bias/kp. Bends add to this, and kp = 2 is probably too weak to hold a bend. Changes: (1) add a small integral term, ki = 0.5, to remove the constant motor-mismatch offset (the integral is capped at +/-2, so it cannot wind up badly); (2) raise kp from 2.0 to 3.0 for stronger correction on bends; (3) keep kd = 0.3, which iteration 1 showed to be well damped; (4) lower base_speed from 1.2 to 1.0 so the robot stays on the line through bends. Finishing time becomes the trade-off, but off-track failure dominates the score now, so completion comes first. Geometry is kept identical to iteration 1 so that the controller change is isolated. Hypotheses: (a) rms_error falls below 0.015 with ki > 0; (b) line_loss_events falls below 0.5 per run; (c) progress on the s-bend exceeds 0.5. If progress rises but the robot still runs off, the next step is to raise kp further. If steering_oscillation rises above about 0.2, reduce kp or raise kd. If the run completes, the next step is to raise base_speed to bring completion_time under 3 s. Expected result: a first partial or full completion on oval and s-bend.
